Sub: Submission of Annual Report for the FY 2025-26 
 
Pursuant to Regulation 34(1) and 53(2) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing Regulations’), please find enclosed herewith the Annual Report of the Company for 
the financial year 2025-26. 
 
The Annual Report is being sent only through electronic mode, to those Members whose e-mail addresses are 
registered with the Company/Registrar and Transfer Agent (RTA)/Depository Participant or Depositories in 
compliance with the applicable SEBI and MCA circulars. 
 
Further, pursuant to Regulation 36(1)(b) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, the Company has initiated dispatch of 
letters to those shareholders whose e-mail addresses are not registered with the Company/RTA/Depositories, 
providing a web-link to access the AGM Notice and Annual Report. 
 
The Annual Report for the Financial Year 2025-26 has also been uploaded on the website of the Company at 
www.narayanahealth.org .  
 
Kindly take the above information on record. 
 
Thanking you

For Narayana Hrudayalaya Limited

Chairman’s Message
Reaching a quarter-century 
is a significant milestone 
for any organization, and it 
gives us a chance to reflect 
on 25 years of resilience, 
achievement, adaptation, 
innovation, and lasting 
societal impact.25 Years of Healthcare Democratization: 
Building the Unassailable Moat
Twenty-six years ago, we began our journey as 
advanced cardiac care providers with just two 
hospitals—the first in Calcutta, quickly followed by 
our second facility in Bangalore.  Over the years, 
we grew to become the single largest cardiac care 
provider in India, performing approximately 16% 
of all major heart surgeries nationwide.Dear Shareholders,
I would like to congratulate all our 
shareholders as we mark our Silver 
Jubilee and celebrate 25 glorious years 
of Narayana Health. Reaching a quarter-
century is a significant milestone for any 
organization, and it gives us a chance 
to reflect on 25 years of resilience, 
achievement, adaptation, innovation, and 
lasting societal impact.
This is a defining moment for us to present 
the formidable competitive moat we have 
created for large-scale expansion in the 
near future.
Peter Thiel, one of the world’s most 
iconic innovators, famously stated: “All 
happy companies are different and each 
one solves a unique problem. All failed 
companies are the same; they fail to 
escape competition.”  The healthcare 
sector today has become a crowded 
“red ocean.”  Everyone is doing the exact 
same thing while claiming to be different.  
When the average occupancy of most 
large hospitals remains stagnant between 
50% and 63%, and the volume of clinical 
procedures across the major hospitals has 
plateaued over the last five years, we know 
a structural crisis is looming.
Let me explain exactly how Narayana 
Health is fundamentally different, and why 
our unique model is built to endure and 
dominate.
A Legacy of Affordable Care:   Thirty-
six years ago, I left England and started 
my career in Calcutta as a heart surgeon.  
My very first patient for a coronary artery 
bypass graft paid H 1.5 lakh.  I am incredibly 
proud to say that, even today, Narayana 
Health receives less than that exact sum for some of our sponsored heart patients.  
We have proven that world-class clinical 
excellence does not require extractive 
pricing.
National Scale in Cardiac Care:   
Twenty-six years ago, we began our 
journey as advanced cardiac care providers 
with just two hospitals—the first in Calcutta, 
quickly followed by our second facility in 
Bangalore.  Over the years, we grew to 
become the single largest cardiac care provider in India, performing approximately

Financial Performance
Narayana Health recorded its highest-ever 
revenue and EBITDA at the Group level 
in FY26, driven by robust performance 
across India, the Cayman Islands and 
our newly acquired UK operations. 
Consolidated operating revenue for FY26 
stood at H 78,960 Mn, a year-on-year

Digital Transformation    
FY26 marked a decisive shift in how 
Narayana Health uses technology — from a 
collection of point solutions to a connected, 
intelligent digital ecosystem spanning 
clinical operations, quality management 
and patient experience. Central to this shift is our transition from a traditional, 
retrospective approach to quality and 
risk management, toward a paperless 
Digital Quality Management System — 
the Quality Intelligence Platform — that 
brings together internal audits, incident 
management, document control, enterprise 
analytics, staff and patient feedback, 
learning and peer review on a single, real-
time platform.
Platforms Driving the 
Transformation   
• OP kiosks: Self-service registration 
is scaling rapidly across hospitals —
to more than 50% of transactions 
— reducing manual front-desk load 
and improving the patient arrival 
experience.  
• Digital Medication Card: Reported 
medication errors dropped by 
96%, following the digitisation  of 
a previously manual, error-prone 
process.
• LIS + Medha and RIS + MedhaX:  
Our in-house laboratory and radiology 
information platforms provide real-time 
tracking of tests and imaging studies, 
automate verification, and integrate 
directly with PACS and EMR.
• ATHMA Hospital Information 
System: Fully integrated incident 
reporting, enabling every event to 
be tracked, investigated and closed 
electronically, and driving a 56% 
increase in total incident reporting as 
a marker of a maturing safety culture.
• AIRO (Enterprise Analytics): Powers 
real-time, cross-hospital visibility 
into quality, safety and operational 
performance, feeding the same Quality 
Intelligence Platform used for audits, 
incidents and document control.
• NIQSA (Narayana Health 
Internal Quality and Safety Audit 
programme): 7,13,034 internal 
audits completed in FY26, a 45% 
increase over the previous year, with 97.7% average compliance; 
the upcoming Audit Bot will add 
automated reminders, escalations and 
a complete digital trail to support 365-
day accreditation readiness
• Knowledge Ecosystem (KES): An 
AI-powered natural-language SOP 
retrieval system within our Document 
Management System, supporting 
96% policy familiarisation across the 
network.
• AMBER platform: Delivers our AI-
enabled AHRQ Survey on Patient 
Safety Culture (SOPS 2.0), achieving 
a 72% response rate and informing 
culture-of-safety interventions.
The intent behind this transformation 
goes beyond automation. By moving from 
periodic, compliance-driven reviews to 
continuous, real-time monitoring, we are 
redefining the role of our Quality function 
— from a team focused on retrospective 
checks to a strategic partner using data and 
predictive analytics to identify and mitigate 
risk before it reaches a patient. This is 
also proving to be a meaningful cost lever: 
reduced administrative workload, fewer 
reworks and harm events, and always-
on accreditation readiness are lowering 
the cost of preventable failure across 
the network, consistent with our broader 
philosophy that the safest care is also the 
most efficient care.

Dr. Devi Prasad Shetty

Dr. Devi Prasad Shetty is the Chairman of our

	 SRCC Children’s Hospital (Narayana Health) Mumbai successfully managed a 2-month-old with a metabolic disorder 
Long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (LCAD) deficiency - a rare inherited metabolic disorder that prevents the body 
from breaking down certain fats for energy that causes severe, life-threatening organ failure. The child was presented 
with severe cardiac failure & coma, and had a high mortality likelihood score. The child was supported and treated for  
> 1 month and is now 5 months old and thriving
	 SRCC Children’s Hospital (Narayana Health) Mumbai successfully managed a 40-day-neonate referred to & diagnosed 
by us to have Methylmalonic acidemia – life threatening metabolic disorder that if not treated early results in brain, liver & 
kidney damage. Ammonia levels rise and dialysis is only partially effective. Team facilitated import of Carglumic acid from 
Europe. Child is doing well and is a candidate for liver transplant in about 6 months

Making Advanced Cancer Care More AccessibleAdvancing Immunotherapy and Cellular Therapies
Expanding access to specialized oncology services remained a key strategic priority during FY26.
Radiation Oncology services were commissioned at Narayana Hospital Mysore and Narayana Hospital Ahmedabad, strengthening 
comprehensive cancer care capabilities across Southern and Western India. Supported by advanced radiation technology and 
precision treatment planning, these centres enable patients to access high-quality radiation therapy closer to home, reducing travel 
burden and supporting continuity of treatment.
A significant milestone during the year was our strategic partnership with Everhope Cancer Centres. Through this collaboration, 
specialized consultations, chemotherapy, diagnostics, supportive care and follow-up services are being brought closer to patients 
within their communities, while remaining connected to Narayana Health’s multidisciplinary oncology network for complex interventions 
when required.
This approach strengthens a coordinated hub-and-spoke model of care, enabling patients to receive the right level of care at the 
most appropriate location while improving accessibility, continuity and convenience.As an established, high-volume centre for haematological cancers, Narayana Health Cancer Care is actively involved in multiple 
pioneering clinical trials evaluating novel immunotherapies and cellular therapies. Alongside offering evidence-based immunotherapy, 
our growing capabilities in CAR-T cell therapy, Bone Marrow Transplantation, molecular diagnostics and precision medicine are 
expanding treatment options for patients with complex blood cancers.

Advancing Precision Oncology
Precision medicine continues to redefine how cancer is diagnosed and treated. During FY26, Narayana Health strengthened its 
Molecular Diagnostic capabilities through the expansion of Next-Generation Sequencing services across Kolkata, Delhi and Bengaluru.
These genomic platforms support comprehensive molecular profiling and help clinicians identify actionable alterations that may inform 
targeted therapies, immunotherapies and individualized treatment strategies based on tumour biology. By integrating advanced 
molecular diagnostics into routine oncology practice, we are improving diagnostic precision, reducing turnaround times and enabling 
faster, evidence-based clinical decisions.

Governance Framework
Excellence begins with strong leadership 
and accountability. Our governance 
framework ensures that safety, quality and Advanced Neurosciences and Interventional Neurology
Advanced Renal, Urology and Gastrointestinal Care
Comprehensive Transplant CareOur Neurosciences program continued to grow in scale and complexity, performing 7,000+ neurosurgeries in FY26 across conditions 
ranging from stroke, epilepsy, and movement disorders & Parkinson’s to Alzheimer’s & dementia and cerebral palsy. The neurosurgical 
segment spans awake brain surgery, brain & spinal tumours, skull base surgery, functional neurosurgeries, minimally invasive surgeries, 
neurosurgical oncology, and several other complex cranial & spine procedures, supported by comprehensive Neurorehabilitation 
and Neuro-Imaging services. As the first centre in India to perform Mechanical Thrombectomy and temporary endovascular bypass 
/ stent retriever procedures for stroke, and to deploy AI-based stroke imaging (the RAPID system), we have established ourselves as 
pioneers in the discipline of Interventional Neurology.
The Nephro-Urology team at Narayana Health is among the most experienced and skilled in the country. Our approach to renal care 
includes diagnosis, treatment, and management of various kidney disorders, including chronic kidney disease (CKD), acute kidney 
injury, dialysis services, kidney transplantation, and post-transplant care. We are also among the first few centres to perform ABO 
incompatible and cadaveric transplants. Our Haemodialysis program supported 387,000+ sessions in FY26. The Urology service 
spectrum encompasses diagnosis and treatment of a wide range of genitourinary conditions across benign and malignant segments, 
with surgical capabilities ranging from laparoscopic to minimally invasive to the most advanced robotic techniques, including andrology,

NARAYANA HEALTH’S EIGHT PILLARS FOR ZERO-HARM HEALTHCAREAt Narayana Health, every patient deserves care that is safe, timely, compassionate and consistently reliable. While no healthcare 
system can eliminate risk, our responsibility is to build systems that minimise harm, prevent avoidable errors and ensure every patient 
receives the best possible care.
Our Zero Harm Framework represents this commitment. It is not a single programme or a short-term initiative. It is a way of thinking 
that shapes how we design our processes, train our people, use technology and continuously improve the care we provide.
The framework is supported by the three foundations of the NASQAR programme. Strong governance provides clear direction and 
accountability. An engaged workforce empowers every member of our team to identify risks, speak up and contribute to safer care. 
Continuous learning ensures that every incident, every audit and every patient experience becomes an opportunity to improve our 
systems for the future.
Working together, these three foundations support eight strategic pillars that guide our efforts across every Narayana Health hospital. 
They cover the entire patient journey, from timely access to care and safe emergency services, to infection prevention, nursing 
excellence, digital innovation, clinical outcomes and continuous learning. Each pillar represents an essential element of delivering 
healthcare that patients can trust.

3.1d — Structured Internal Audit
Regular internal audits help ensure that every hospital consistently delivers safe, high-quality care. These audits are carried out using 
a fully digital system that plans, tracks and follows each audit from start to finish, ensuring that no review is missed.
Using standard checklists based on national and international accreditation standards, trained auditors assess different aspects of 
patient care and hospital operations. Any gaps identified are recorded immediately, prioritised according to risk and followed through 
with corrective actions until they are resolved.
This structured approach helps us maintain consistent standards across all our hospitals, strengthens patient safety, improves quality 
of care, enhances operational efficiency and supports a culture of continuous improvement.
Our internal audit programme is organised into eight key categories, covering all critical aspects of clinical and operational performance.

3.1g — Code Blue and Rapid Response Teams — Responding Early, Saving Lives
Code Blue and Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) are critical components of the hospital’s emergency response system. While RRTs 
enable early recognition and intervention for deteriorating patients, Code Blue teams provide immediate, coordinated resuscitation 
following cardiac or respiratory arrest. Together, they strengthen the continuum of care from early identification of deterioration to 
timely emergency response and resuscitation.
The data demonstrates a consistently responsive emergency care system across the Group. The high number of RRT activations 
also reflects the importance of early recognition and escalation of deteriorating patients. Continued focus on early warning systems, 
timely RRT activation, regular resuscitation training, Code Blue reviews and analysis of potentially preventable cardiac arrests will 
further strengthen outcomes and advance the goal of preventing avoidable deterioration and harm.
During FY26, 10,642 RRT calls and 5,267 Code Blue activations were recorded across 
the network. The average team arrival time was 3 minutes 28 seconds, remaining 
within the target of five minutes, while the average time to initiate CPR was 51 
seconds. Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) was achieved in 56% of Code 
Blue events. Monthly ROSC rates remained relatively stable, ranging from 50% to 
62%, without a sustained decline during the year.

3.1f — Mock Drill — Preparing for the Moments That MatterIn a High Reliability Organisation, incident reporting is one of the strongest indicators of a healthy safety culture. The goal is not to 
identify who made a mistake, but to understand why it happened and prevent it from happening again. Every incident, near miss 
and unsafe condition provides an opportunity to strengthen systems, improve processes and make care safer for future patients.
At Narayana Health, we actively encourage staff to report incidents through a simple, transparent and non-punitive reporting system. 
Every report is reviewed, investigated where required, and translated into corrective and preventive actions. Lessons learnt are shared 
across the organisation, ensuring that improvements benefit every hospital.
Emergencies are unpredictable, but our response should never be. At Narayana Health, regular mock drills help ensure that when a real 
emergency occurs, our teams are prepared to respond quickly, confidently and in a coordinated manner. These simulated exercises 
allow doctors, nurses and support teams to practise managing situations such as cardiac arrest, fire, major bleeding, disasters and 
security incidents in a safe, controlled environment.
Mock drills help identify gaps in equipment, communication, infrastructure and emergency processes before they affect patient care. 
They also strengthen teamwork, clarify individual roles and improve response times when every second matters. Regular practice 
builds confidence and helps ensure that patients receive safe, timely and effective care during critical situations.
Drills are conducted throughout the year at frequencies based on risk, ensuring our teams remain ready to respond effectively 
whenever patients need us most.These trends are hallmarks of a maturing safety culture, where staff feel empowered to speak up, learn from every event and 
continuously improve the quality and safety of care.Facility & Safety 41,820

3.1i — Governance Framework — Working Together for Safer Care
Clinical, Quality and Diagnostic Governance Framework Facility Safety Management Governance FrameworkChaperone – Protecting Dignity, Privacy and TrustPatient Safety Rounds (PSR) are structured two-hourly nursing rounds designed to proactively address patient needs and prevent 
avoidable harm. During each round, nurses assess the 4 Ps – Pain, Position, Potty Needs and Placement of essential items, whilst 
also identifying immediate safety and comfort concerns. For patients, this means regular attention, timely assistance and reassurance 
that their needs are anticipated rather than waiting for them to seek help. This proactive approach enhances comfort, reduces the 
risk of falls and other preventable harm, and strengthens the overall patient experience.
With sustained compliance of over 98%, Patient Safety Rounds demonstrate how a simple, structured and consistently applied 
practice can embed safety into everyday care, ensuring that every patient is seen, supported and protected.
Delivering safe, high-quality healthcare requires every part of the organisation to work together. At Narayana Health, our five-level 
governance framework brings together doctors, nurses, allied health professionals, administrators, quality teams, facility management 
and the Board in a structured process of review, learning and improvement.
The framework consists of two complementary governance streams. One focuses on clinical quality, patient safety and diagnostic 
excellence, while the other oversees facility safety, infrastructure and operational preparedness. At every level, teams regularly review 
performance, discuss challenges, share learning and monitor progress on improvement actions.At Narayana Health, all staff undergo mandatory chaperone training to ensure a consistent understanding of patient dignity, privacy, 
consent and professional boundaries. Where indicated, chaperone is present during sensitive examinations and procedures, providing 
patients with reassurance and support while adding an important layer of transparency and accountability to the care being delivered.

3.2a — Laboratory Quality Assurance — Right Results, Right Time
3.2b — Transfusion Medicine — Blood Transfusion SafetyEvery diagnosis and treatment decision depends on laboratory results that are accurate and available on time. In 2025, Narayana Health 
laboratories processed in excess of 10 million samples, each representing a patient waiting for an answer that could guide their care.
More than 99.5% of laboratory test runs met the required standards for accuracy and precision. This means fewer repeat tests and 
blood draws, greater confidence in results, and timely treatment decisions. Our performance is also regularly compared with national 
and international laboratories. 
Safe blood transfusion depends on ensuring that the right blood reaches the right patient at the right time. Our digital Blood Bank 
Module connects the entire transfusion journey-from requesting blood and checking inventory to patient identification, crossmatching, 
issue, transfusion and monitoring, reducing manual processes and opportunities for error.
During FY26, blood and blood products were issued in an average of 47 minutes, with turnaround times remaining consistently 
between 44 and 51 minutes. Transfusion reactions remained low at 0.1% and adverse donor reactions at 0.4%. By strengthening 
patient identification and introducing digital checks at every stage, the Blood Bank Module has helped reduce errors and improve 
the safety, traceability and reliability of blood transfusion across the Group.Some laboratory results are needed urgently. During cancer surgery, for example, a surgeon may pause the procedure while a 
pathologist examines a tissue sample to help determine the next step. In FY26, 99% of these frozen section results were reported 
within 30 minutes, helping surgeons make timely decisions while the patient was still in the operating theatre.
In FY26, across 11,568 external quality assessment tests, the outlier rate was just 0.90%.

“How often did we get it right the first time?”The framework shifts the conversation from measuring defects to measuring 
reliability. Instead of only asking “How many errors occurred?”, teams begin asking 
“How often did we get it right the first time?”. This aligns with NH’s aspirations for 
Zero Harm, clinical excellence and high reliability and is set to become a core pillar of 
the Clinical Governance programme.Why DRFT matters“Do It Right First Time” is a simple, memorable way of bringing together quality, safety, efficiency and waste reduction. The philosophy 
is that every process should be planned, prepared, performed correctly and completed safely the first time, avoiding repeat procedures, 
patient harm, delays and unnecessary cost.
Do It Right First Time (DRFT) is Narayana Health’s philosophy for delivering healthcare that is safe, reliable and consistently excellent. 
It is based on a simple principle: every patient should receive the right care, at the right time, in the right way, the first time. By getting 
processes right from the outset, we reduce avoidable errors, unnecessary investigations, repeat procedures, delays and waste, while 
improving outcomes and the patient experience.
As Narayana Health continues its journey towards Zero Harm Healthcare, DRFT will become a core pillar of our Clinical Governance 
programme, bringing together patient safety, quality, operational excellence and continuous improvement into one shared way of working. For patients, DRFT means safer care, fewer complications, shorter hospital stays and less need for repeat tests or procedures. 
 For our healthcare teams, it provides clear, standardised processes that reduce variation, support better clinical decisions and  
 allow more time to focus on patient care. 
 For the organisation, it improves efficiency, reduces unnecessary costs and makes better use of resources without   
 compromising quality.
 DRFT is a cornerstone of a High Reliability Organisation, where excellence is measured not simply by how well we recover  
 from errors, but by how consistently we prevent them from occurring. Rather than asking, “How many mistakes did we  
 make?”, DRFT asks a more powerful question:

PILLAR 3.3 — TIMELY ACCESS TO EMERGENCY & 
ELECTIVE CARE
When someone experiences a medical emergency, every minute counts. Rapid access to the right treatment can save lives, reduce 
complications and improve recovery. Timely care also means minimising waiting times for investigations, laboratory tests and planned 
procedures, ensuring patients receive the care they need without unnecessary delays.
At Narayana Health, we continuously monitor key time-based indicators across emergency and elective care. These include treatment 
pathways for stroke, heart attack, sepsis and major bleeding, as well as emergency department waiting times, laboratory turnaround 
times and surgical scheduling. Monitoring these measures helps us identify opportunities to improve and ensures we consistently 
deliver safe, high-quality care.
Performance remained strong across most time critical pathways. Stroke patients received clot dissolving treatment within an average 
of 44 minutes, well within the 60-minute benchmark, while 99.5% of patients received the RAPID Sepsis care bundle on time. The 
average emergency department length of stay was 192 minutes, only 2.5% of planned surgeries were rescheduled, and 91% of 
laboratory tests met the defined turnaround time.
The average Door to Balloon time for patients with a heart attack was 98 minutes, compared with the international benchmark of 90 
minutes or less. Improving this remains an important focus area, and targeted initiatives are underway to further reduce treatment 
times and ensure patients receive lifesaving interventions as quickly as possible.
This approach demonstrates a key principle of Narayana Health’s governance programme: we celebrate areas of excellence while 
openly measuring, reporting and improving areas where better outcomes are still possible.

3.4a Antimicrobial Stewardship. Using Antibiotics Wisely
Antibiotics save lives, but they must be used carefully. Using the wrong antibiotic, or using them for longer than necessary, can lead 
to side effects and the development of antibiotic resistance, making future infections more difficult to treat. Antimicrobial Stewardship 
(AMS) is our programme to ensure every patient receives the right antibiotic, at the right dose, at the right time, for the right duration. 
This approach helps patients recover faster, reduces unnecessary exposure to antibiotics and protects these lifesaving medicines 
for future generations.
Narayana Health demonstrated excellent antibiotic stewardship across almost all measures. More than 99% of patients undergoing 
surgery received preventive antibiotics at the correct time, and 98.6% received the most appropriate antibiotic, helping reduce the risk 
of surgical infections. For patients requiring restricted or high potency antibiotics, 98.9% had a clear clinical indication documented, 
and 94.7% had blood cultures taken before treatment, ensuring the antibiotic was targeted to the infection whenever possible.
Every patient’s need for antibiotics was reviewed within 72 hours (100%), preventing unnecessary prolonged treatment. Compliance 
with narrowing or changing antibiotics once culture results became available was 87.1%, slightly below our target of 90%, and 
remains an important area for improvement.
These results demonstrate our commitment to using antibiotics responsibly, improving patient outcomes today while helping combat 
the growing global challenge of antimicrobial resistance for the future.Key Findings

CONTROL — EVERYONE’S RESPONSIBILITY
Preventing infections is one of the most important ways we keep our patients safe. At Narayana Health, infection prevention is not 
the responsibility of one team alone. It is a shared commitment embraced by every doctor, nurse, technician, support staff member, 
patient and visitor. From hand hygiene and cleaning practices to the safe use of medical devices and antibiotics, every action plays 
a part in preventing infections.
Many serious hospitals acquired infections are preventable. By consistently following internationally recognised care bundles and 
evidence-based practices, we reduce the risk of infections related to ventilators, urinary catheters, central lines and surgery. This 
means fewer complications, shorter hospital stays, faster recovery and better outcomes for our patients.
Narayana Health achieved 98 to 99% compliance with infection prevention care bundles across all major areas, demonstrating 
excellent adherence to best practices.
These results reflect the collective efforts of our teams in making infection prevention part of everyday practice. Every clean pair of 
hands, every correctly followed protocol and every timely intervention contribute to safer care and better outcomes for our patients.

3.6c — Operation Theatre Safety — Safe Surgery at Every StepPatients in the Intensive Care Unit are among the sickest in the hospital. These measures help ensure they receive timely treatment, 
appropriate nutrition, early rehabilitation and safe transfer out of intensive care.What this means for our patients
Patients admitted to our Intensive Care Units received care that consistently met or exceeded national and international benchmarks. 
The Standardised Mortality Ratio (SMR) of 0.39 means that significantly fewer patients died than would be expected based on how 
seriously ill they were, reflecting excellent critical care outcomes.
Patients were safely weaned from ventilators, with only 3.2% requiring breathing support again within 48 hours, well below the target 
of 10%. Recovery was actively supported, with 99.4% of patients mobilised early and 98.5% receiving timely nutritional support, 
both of which are proven to reduce complications, preserve strength and speed recovery.
Surgery involves many critical steps, and patient safety depends on careful preparation, clear communication and teamwork. In 
FY26, 95,568 surgical procedures were performed across the Group, with strong compliance with essential safety practices. Pre-
anaesthetic assessment compliance was 99.57%, Sign In and Time Out compliance exceeded 98%, and timely antibiotic prophylaxis 
compliance was 98.90%. These checks help ensure that it is the right patient, the right procedure and the right surgical site, while 
reducing the risk of infection and other preventable complications.
Key surgical outcomes also remained strong, with cancellations at 2.2%, rescheduling at 2.5%, return to the operation theatre at 
0.6%, and adverse anaesthesia events at 0.11%. Monitoring these measures helps us reduce delays and cancellations, identify 
opportunities for improvement and learn from every unexpected event, making surgery safer and the overall patient experience better.
Lower is better for re-scheduling, cancellation, return to OT and adverse anaesthesia events; all four remain well controlled against

Quality management at Narayana Health is a continuous commitment to ensuring that every patient receives safe, effective, timely 
and compassionate care. Traditionally, this has been built on well-defined policies, clinical audits, incident reporting, accreditation 
standards and governance processes that established a strong foundation for quality and patient safety.
However, these approaches were largely manual, retrospective and compliance driven. Information was often spread across paper 
records and spreadsheets, risks became visible only after events had occurred, and considerable effort was spent preparing for 
periodic inspections rather than continuously improving everyday practice.
As healthcare becomes increasingly complex, high volume and data driven, quality management must evolve beyond periodic review. 
It requires a proactive approach where quality, safety and risk are continuously monitored, measured and acted upon in real time, 
enabling earlier identification of risks, faster decision making and more consistent, reliable care for every patient.PILLAR 3.8 — QUALITY MANAGEMENT SYSTEM
3.8a — Transforming Quality Through a Connected, Intelligent Digital Ecosystem
To meet these evolving demands, Narayana Health is transitioning from a traditional quality management approach to an intelligent, 
integrated and paperless Digital Quality Management System. Rather than relying on isolated systems and manual processes, all 
quality activities including audits, incident reporting, document control, analytics, patient feedback, staff experience, learning, peer 
review and accreditation are brought together on a single connected platform.
This transformation enables quality, safety and risk to be monitored continuously rather than periodically, providing real time visibility 
of performance across every hospital. It also redefines the role of the Quality Department from one focused primarily on compliance 
and retrospective reviews to a strategic partner that uses data and insights to drive safer care, faster improvement and better 
outcomes for every patient.

At Narayana Health, every mortality is an opportunity to learn and improve. As part of our commitment to Zero Harm, over 95% of 
mortalities are reviewed each month through a Structured Mortality Review process, using a standardised, analytics-enabled framework 
adapted from global best practices of the IHI and WHO.
The review looks beyond the immediate cause of death to examine the entire patient journey, identifying clinical and system-level 
factors that may have contributed to the outcome. Triggers such as Code Blue events, infections, readmissions, adverse drug events, 
re-intubation, return to the operation theatre and other complications help identify opportunities to make care safer.
Findings are discussed through our Clinical Governance Framework, translated into improvement actions and shared across the 
Group so that learning from one patient can improve care for many others. 3.7b — Mortality Reviews — Learning from Every Death, Striving for Zero Harm

Every preventable infection, medication error, delayed diagnosis, repeat procedure or prolonged hospital stay carries a cost, not only

Our focus is therefore simple: Do It Right First Time. By building reliable systems that prevent errors, reduce variation and improve 
consistency, we minimise waste, avoid unnecessary interventions and make the best use of people, time and resources. Better quality

The safest and most reliable care is often the most efficient and cost effective.Narayana Health Risk Management Programme (NRM)3.8b — Quality Process Highlights
Narayana Health Internal Quality and Safety Audit Programme (NIQSA)
At Narayana Health, managing risk means identifying potential problems before they affect our patients. Every year, all hospitals carry 
out proactive risk assessments across key areas such as medication safety, infection prevention, diagnostics and facility management. 
The findings are used to implement a group wide programme that reduces risks and strengthens patient safety.
Incident reporting is fully integrated into our ATHMA Hospital Information System (HIS), making it easy for staff to report incidents 
electronically, ensuring every event is tracked, investigated and followed through to completion. This digital approach has significantly 
increased the reporting of incidents, enabling earlier identification of risks and faster action to prevent recurrence.
A key strength of our programme is the reporting of near misses. These are situations where a potential error is identified before it 
reaches the patient. By learning from these events, we can improve our systems and prevent harm before it occurs. More than 90% 
of reported incidents are investigated and closed within the defined service timelines, ensuring timely learning, effective root cause 
analysis and continuous improvement across the organisation.At Narayana Health, quality is continuously monitored through the Narayana Health Internal Quality and Safety Audit (NIQSA) 
programme. Trained multidisciplinary auditors conduct comprehensive, cross functional and cross hospital audits using standardised 
checklists covering International Patient Safety Goals (IPSG), medical record documentation, clinical processes and facility safety.
Every stage of the audit process, from planning and scheduling to reporting, corrective actions and closure, is managed through a 
single digital platform, ensuring consistency across all hospitals and continuous accreditation readiness.
During FY26, Narayana Health completed 7,13,034 internal audits, a 45% increase over the 
previous year, while maintaining an impressive 97.7% average compliance.
The introduction of the Audit Bot will further strengthen the programme through automated 
reminders, timely escalations and a complete digital audit trail, enabling continuous 
monitoring and supporting 365-day quality and accreditation readiness

CLINICAL RESEARCH AT NARAYANA HEALTH 
Research remained a defining pillar of Narayana Health’s academic identity in FY 2025–26, with the Group deepening its infrastructure, 
expanding external partnerships, and earning wider national and international recognition for the quality of its output.
Building Research Infrastructure and Partnerships
Research Output and Researcher Support
Recognitions and HonoursFY 2025–26 saw considerable expansion in the research infrastructure and external partnerships underpinning Narayana Health’s 
academic ambitions. The Group has filed grant applications in partnership with the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), entered a 
partnership with Microsoft for AI-based research. Additional ICMR grant applications were also filed jointly with Mazumdar Shaw 
Medical Foundation (MSMF). Narayana Health also served as the principal site for the multi-centric Perceval valve study, and a formal 
policy was established governing the extraction and sharing of data for research. Institutional Review Board / Ethics Committee (IRB/
EC) coverage now extends to seven units, with the process under way at Raipur and Mysore, while work continued on building out 
the NH Bio-Bank and the Narayana Clinical Research India Foundation (NCRIF).
The quality of the Group’s research output continued to rise, with an average impact factor of 2.67 across publications and nine 
papers appearing in journals with an impact factor above 10. To sustain this momentum, Narayana Health provided INR 25 lakhs in 
researcher support during the year, comprising INR 14.1 lakhs in cash incentives for publications and conference participation and 
INR 10.9 lakhs in institutional support for investigations.
Narayana Health’s research programme received significant national and international recognition in 2025. According to a paper 
published in the Indian Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery, the group was seen as a leading private hospital group 
in India for cardiac surgical research in the country. Dr. Satish Govind presented an abstract at the American Heart Association 
Scientific Sessions 2025 in New Orleans, and the network’s cardiovascular research earned a Paul Dudley White International 
Scholar recognition. Narayana Health’s cardiac surgery team won Best Paper at the Annual Conference of the Indian Association of 
Cardiovascular-Thoracic Surgeons for the fourth consecutive year and published the largest Indian series on the Ross Procedure in 
the Annals of Thoracic Surgery. Researchers presented at several major international meetings during the year, including abstracts at 
the European Crohn’s and Colitis Organisation Congress 2026 in Stockholm, the European Atherosclerosis Society 2026, the Society 
for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions Conference in the USA, and at the Young Cardiologists’ Session presentation at 
Asian Pacific Society of Cardiology Congress at  Japan. The National Board also commended outstanding theses by Dr. Shreya Garg 
(DNB, Endovascular & Interventional Radiology), Dr. Mohammed Roshan Zameer (Cardiac Surgery), and Dr. Dobariya Jitendrakumar 
Bavchandbhai (Cardiac Surgery) .

Reimagining Access, Affordability, and Accountability in Indian Healthcare
The Evolving Economics of Healthcare in India
As one of the world’s largest and most populous nations, with approximately 1.4 billion 
people (18% of the global population), India’s health outcomes have far-reaching 
implications for both national and global health indicators. India is now entering a decisive 
execution phase in its healthcare evolution, transitioning from historical underinvestment 
toward more structured and sustained expansion.
Management Discussion 
& Analysis-FY26
Statutory Reports
Corporate Overview Financial Statements
63

=== page 36 ===
However, at approximately ₹1.06 lakh crore allocation for 
healthcare, around 2% of the Union Budget for FY27 it 
continues to trail global benchmarks. This structural gap is not 
merely a constraint; it represents a significant opportunity for 
scalable, cost-efficient private sector models to complement 
public provisioning through innovative financing and 
delivery mechanisms.
At the same time, India stands at a pivotal moment in its journey 
toward universal health coverage, a cornerstone of the Viksit 
Bharat 2047 vision. Backed by strong political intent and 
sustained economic growth, the current environment presents 
a time-bound opportunity to accelerate systemic reforms and 
unlock significant unmet healthcare demand, particularly across 
the underinsured and middle-income segments. This evolving 
landscape is expected to expand the role of integrated, cost-
efficient private healthcare platforms that can bridge the gap 
between affordability and access.
Source: https://www.indiabudget.gov.in
From Fragmentation to a Layered Coverage Architecture
India’s healthcare financing framework is increasingly taking the 
shape of a layered, pragmatic ecosystem one that reflects both 
economic realities and demographic diversity.
• Affluent and organized-sector populations are 
well penetrated by employer-led and private 
insurance arrangements.
• Economically vulnerable groups are progressively 
protected by government-sponsored health assurance 
programs that are increasing both in scale and scope.
• The underserved middle income segment, however, 
remains exposed often earning too much to qualify for 
state support, yet lacking adequate risk protection against 
healthcare shocks.
This “missing middle” continues to bear a disproportionate share 
of healthcare costs through direct out-of-pocket expenditure, 
limiting timely care and exacerbating financial stress. Bridging 
this gap is essential to unlocking true healthcare inclusion.
This gap persists despite nearly four decades of voluntary health 
insurance, which, as of 2023–24, covers only 312 million people 
(21.5% of the population), with coverage largely concentrated 
among employer-linked beneficiaries, underscoring the need for 
targeted interventions to achieve inclusive financial protection.
Source: The Lancet Commission report, 2026
Aditi: Converting Insurance from a Barrier into an Enabler
During FY26, Narayana Health continued to scale Narayana 
Aditi, our purpose-built health insurance product for the 
missing middle. Designed around simplicity, predictability, 
and affordability, Aditi challenges the traditional insurance paradigm by tightly integrating clinical care delivery with 
financial protection.
With a modest monthly premium structure and high coverage 
limits for families, Aditi is not positioned as a transactional 
insurance offering-but as a long-term healthcare partnership. 
As adoption expands, we see Aditi playing a pivotal role in 
reshaping how Indian families engage with preventive care, 
elective procedures, and long-term health planning.
Insurance Growth Meets a Trust Deficit
India’s health insurance segment maintained strong momentum 
in FY26, reporting ~15% year on year growth to reach a record 
gross written premium of ₹1.37 lakh crore. The expansion 
was primarily driven by strong traction in retail health policies 
following the GST rate reduction implemented in late FY25, 
alongside robust renewal performance, with persistency levels 
reaching all time highs during the year.
Source: https://www.financialexpress.com
Yet this growth co-exists with persistent skepticism. 
Policyholders frequently encounter opaque exclusions, 
inconsistent care pathways, and unexpected expenses leading 
to a trust deficit that restricts deeper penetration.
At Narayana Health, we believe this trust gap can only be 
addressed by re-engineering incentives not by incremental 
fixes. Our response has been to tightly align medical decision-
making, cost structures, and patient outcomes within a single, 
accountable ecosystem.
Underwriting is a core component of our health insurance 
operations, underpinning effective risk assessment and long-
term sustainability. For retail indemnity products, including 
Narayana Aditi, Arya Health Insurance and individually 
underwritten group affinity offerings, at Narayan health we 
follow a structured medical and lifestyle underwriting framework 
based on declared information, questionnaires and medical 
examinations, where applicable. This approach enables 
informed risk evaluation and appropriate structuring of policy 
terms while supporting prudent and responsible expansion of 
health insurance coverage.
Embedding Clinical Accountability at Scale
In India, an estimated 1.6 million deaths annually are attributed to 
poor quality of care, exceeding those caused by lack of access, 
highlighting the critical importance of clinical governance and 
standardisation.
Source: The Lancet Commission report, 2026
Our integrated care model places clinical governance at 
its core. During FY26, we further strengthened enterprise-
wide mechanisms to ensure consistency, transparency, and 
evidence-based decision-making:

Global Diversification and Domestic Capacity Expansion
As part of our long-term growth strategy, Narayana Health 
expanded its global footprint with the acquisition of UK 
based Practice Plus Group Hospitals in FY26. Practice Plus 
Group, the fifth largest private hospital group in the UK, 
operates 12 hospitals and surgical centres and performs 
approximately 80,000 surgeries annually across specialties 
such as orthopaedics, ophthalmology and general surgery. 
This strategic investment reflects a measured approach to 
geographic diversification, enabling the Company to access a 
stable, mature healthcare market while mitigating concentration 
risk and enhancing revenue resilience. It also provides exposure 
to differentiated operating environments and payer systems.
In India, the Company’s expansion continues to be guided by 
a disciplined capacity creation agenda aligned with strategic 
intent. All previously committed projects are progressing as 
planned, supporting the scaled augmentation of infrastructure 
in line with demand growth and network optimisation priorities.
We continue to view physical infrastructure as an outcome of 
strategy, not its driver. Each expansion decision is evaluated 
through the lens of clinical capability, digital integration, and 
ecosystem synergies.
Technology as Core Infrastructure
Technology continued to be the defining backbone of Narayana 
Health’s operating model in FY26.
Our digital platforms Athma and Medha advanced from 
efficiency tools into strategic assets. Athma further unified 
clinical, administrative, and patient engagement workflows, 
increasing self-service adoption and reducing friction across 
touchpoints. Patient-led digital engagement now constitutes a 
majority of outpatient interactions.
Clinical productivity gains accelerated through:
• OPD Digitalisation
• Automation of documentation and discharge workflows
• Upgradation of the ATHMA website and launch of a SaaS-
based patient portal• Launch of the One Health Plan Manager
• Mobile-first tools for doctors and nurses
Collectively, these initiatives demonstrate Narayana Health’s 
continued commitment to digital excellence and scalability, 
while delivering measurable improvements in turnaround 
times, workforce utilisation, and consistency of patient care 
across the network.
Medha’s expanding analytics capabilities are enabling more 
personalized care pathways, predictive risk identification, and 
continuous outcome feedback laying the groundwork for true 
value-based healthcare.
AI-Led Intelligence Transformation
During FY26, Narayana Health advanced its AI strategy 
through a structured intelligence maturity framework spanning 
foundational, actionable, and agentic intelligence, with a unified 
data layer enabling a single source of truth across operations. 
Building on this, targeted use cases such as revenue leakage, 
clinical care gaps, and cash optimization were embedded into 
workflows and tracked for ROI. We have deployed 40+ bots 
across patients, clinicians, payors, and back-office functions, 
with patient-facing solutions managing over 35,000 daily 
interactions and clinical AI tools enhancing diagnosis and 
documentation (including ECG AI and AI scribe with 2.5 lakh 
documents completed). Agentic systems are increasingly 
enabling automated monitoring and decision support across 
demand planning, clinical workflows, and discharge processes.
This disciplined, outcome-driven approach has delivered 
tangible impact, including savings of over 100,000 clinical hours, 
~40% reduction in inventory days, and cost efficiencies through 
automation of medical coding and administrative processes, 
while also advancing scalable, non-invasive screening solutions 
for early disease detection.
Outlook
India’s healthcare transformation is no longer a question of 
intent but of execution at scale. As demand rises and complexity 
deepens, the system will increasingly reward models that 
combine affordability with accountability.
Narayana Health enters FY27 with a clear strategic conviction: 
the future belongs to integrated platforms that align incentives 
across prevention, care delivery, and financing. By embedding 
trust, technology, and transparency into every layer of care, we 
aim not just to participate in India’s healthcare evolution, but 
to help shape it.
Our focus remains steadfast delivering clinically excellent, 
financially accessible, and deeply human healthcare to every 
family we serve.

Analysis of NH India Hospitals revenue growth and margin performance
Particulars Analysis
Operating Revenue The India hospitals has reported a 10% year-over-year (YoY) increase in revenue, marking a 
significant milestone in its financial performance. This growth is primarily attributed to three 
key factors:
1. Improved Payor Mix: The overall payor mix has shown a positive shift during the period, 
with a higher contribution from cash and general walk-in and Insurance segment 
patients. This improvement reflects stronger direct patient inflow, reduced dependency 
on institutional or credit-based payors, and enhanced revenue quality with quicker 
realizations.
2. Enhanced Realisation Rates: There has been a notable improvement in realization rates, 
driven by a 9% increase in ARPIP (Average Revenue Per In-Patient) compared to the 
previous year. This growth has been supported by a favourable payor mix, including 
higher contributions from cash/general walk-in patients, insurance, and CGHS segments. 
3. Case mix: The case mix has evolved towards higher-value and more complex cases, 
leading to improved revenue per patient. A greater proportion of specialized procedures 
and treatments has contributed to better utilization of clinical capabilities and 
infrastructure, thereby enhancing overall profitability and operational efficiency.
 Together, these factors reflect the hospital’s continued focus on financial sustainability, 
quality care delivery and strategic growth. The outlook remains positive as the institution 
builds on these gains through further innovation and operational excellence.
Consumption Hospital consumption efficiency improved by 6 basis points (bps) year-over-year, reflecting 
enhanced cost control and resource optimization. This improvement is indicative of 
better inventory management, reduced wastage, and more efficient utilization of medical 
consumables.
The gain underscores ongoing efforts to streamline operations and drive margin enhancement 
through disciplined consumption practices.
Employee Benefit expenses and 
Professional fees to Doctors’In FY26, Employee Benefits Expenses and Professional Fees to Doctors accounted for 
38.2% of revenue, an improvement from 39.4% in FY25, despite an increase in absolute 
costs from ₹ 16,961 million to ₹ 18,101 million.
This modest improvement in the cost ratio reflects operating leverage, with revenue growth 
outpacing the rise in Employee-related expenses.
The increase in absolute costs was primarily driven by:
	 Higher payouts to doctors, including continued investment in clinical talent.
	  Annual appraisals and salary revisions aligned with market benchmarks and employee 
retention strategies.
The improved ratio highlights the hospital’s ability to manage workforce costs efficiently while 
continuing to invest in talent and incentivize performance.

administrative ExpensesHospital Other Operational and Administrative Expenses increased from ₹ 7,833 million

leverage and continued cost discipline. Key contributors include:
1. Marketing Cost:
 Reduced by ₹ 129 million, driven by more focused and strategic campaign planning 
base, Improved targeting based on revenue achievements and prioritization of high-
impact channels led to better utilization of marketing spend.
2. Housekeeping Expenses:
 Rose from ₹ 872.3 million (2.03%) to ₹ 962.20 million (2.03%), primary driven by minimum 
wage increases across states.
3. Rentals:
 Increased from ₹ 1,040.30 million (2.4%) to ₹ 1,175.60 million (2.5%) excluding the impact 
of IND AS 116, due to incremental revenue share arrangements and annual escalations.
4. Repairs and Maintenance:
 Grew from ₹ 1,571.9 million (3.65%) FY25 to ₹ 1,697.92 million (3.59%) FY26, reflecting 
ongoing infrastructure upkeep. Though as a % of revenue it is reduced.
5. Rates and Taxes
 Increase in Rates and taxes from ₹ 43.02 million (0.1%) to ₹109.89 million (0.23%), due 
to MMRHL and NHIC Merger stamp duty fees ₹45 million and ₹8 million respectively.
6. Printing & Stationary:
 Reduced from ₹198.95 million in FY25 (0.45%) to ₹ 168.1 million in FY26 (0.35%), Primary 
due to various digital initiates taken by the Company.

effective cost management by maintaining or reducing expenditure in other components.

reinvestment in operations.
Other Income Other Income recorded a 43% year-over-year growth, largely driven by returns from short-term

NH Integrated Care
Narayana Health’s Integrated Care business continued to build on the foundation laid in FY24. With 11 points of presence (clinics)

The Integrated Care model remains a strategic pillar for Narayana Health, aimed at delivering accessible, preventive, and continuous 
care. The early success and rapid scale-up reinforce confidence in its potential to become a significant value driver in the years ahead.

Learning & Development at Narayana Health: 
Investing in Our People, Advancing Our Mission
At Narayana Health, we believe that clinical excellence and 
compassionate care begin with a future-ready workforce. Our 
commitment is to invest purposefully in the holistic development 
of every associate, because in healthcare, capability directly 
translates to patient outcomes. Our learning and development 
ecosystem is designed to empower associates to upskill, adapt 
to rapid medical and technological advancements, and deliver 
measurable impact at the point of care.
Through a blended approach of classroom programs, virtual 
learning, and digital modules, we deliver competency-based 
development that is relevant, accessible, and aligned to evolving 
healthcare needs. Beyond internal offerings, we actively support 
associates in pursuing external certifications, participate in 
conferences, and get nominated in domain-specific programs. 
This ensures our people remain at the forefront of clinical 
protocols, healthcare innovations, and industry best practices 
— enabling them to serve patients with greater confidence, 
safety, and expertise.
Enabling Continuous Learning at Scale
To strengthen a culture of continuous learning at Narayana 
Health, EdSpark — our Digital Learning Management System 
— has expanded significantly in both reach and capability this 
year. The platform now supports a wider associate base through 
an enriched portfolio of curated, competency-based learning 
pathways. EdSpark delivers a seamless, self-directed learning 
experience with asynchronous, multi-device access, enabling 
associates to access learning content at their convenience.
The platform hosts diverse knowledge repositories spanning 
clinical operational programmes, non-clinical programmes, 
functional programmes, programmes on business skills, 
compliance, and other domain related material. These are 
provided through e-books, and podcasts, empowering 
associates to take ownership of their professional growth.

mission of delivering high-quality, affordable healthcare.Recruitment
Recruitment during FY26 was guided by a strategic shift towards 
capability-led hiring and centralised execution, in line with the 
organisation’s broader focus on manpower optimisation and 
cost discipline amidst a competitive healthcare talent market.
A key initiative during the year was the introduction of the 
Talent Acquisition Shared Services (TASS) model, moving 
away from decentralised, unit-led hiring to a centralised, 
pod-based structure. The model aims to improve recruitment 
efficiency through shared talent pools, process standardisation, 
and enhanced visibility of manpower demand across units. The 
Health City pilot, launched in January 2026, has demonstrated 
early improvements in recruiter utilisation and process control, 
and will serve as the basis for a phased enterprise-wide rollout.
Hiring during the year remained selective and investment-
driven, focused on critical roles, leadership positions, 
and future-ready capabilities, while overall headcount 
rationalisation continued. Leadership hiring was addressed 
through a balanced approach of internal talent movement and 
targeted external recruitment.
The organisation continued to emphasise internal talent 
mobility as a key lever for both role fulfilment and retention, 
thereby strengthening the leadership pipeline and reducing 
dependency on external hiring.
The Management Trainee (MT) programmes across 
Operations, Finance, and Supply Chain remained a cornerstone 
for building future talent. These programmes saw strong 
deployment across units, with trainees contributing effectively 
to evolving operational requirements. Retention levels have 
remained stable at approximately 70%, reflecting continued 
programme relevance despite market competition.
Overall, recruitment in FY26 reflects a transition from volume-
driven hiring to a more strategic, capability-focused 
talent acquisition approach, anchored on centralisation, 
selective hiring, and investment in internal and early-career 
talent pipelines. This positions the organisation to enhance 
hiring efficiency while building a sustainable and future-
ready workforce.

We believe that a well-designed reward framework plays a

Risk and Concerns
NH leadership believes that continuous and timely investment 
in people, process and right technology to identify, monitor 
and mitigate critical risks is non-negotiable. Sustained and 
profitable growth is possible only with a complete 360 degree 
view of the overall business risk milieu. The formulation of a 
comprehensive risk strategy and robust mitigation actions are 
key differentiators in our journey toward sustainable excellence.
1. Cybersecurity and Data Privacy
 Cyber risks continue to be the industry wide top concern. 
NH continues to invest in best-in-class technology, 
infrastructure and processes to attain and maintain the 
optimal security posture. Our early investments to comply 
with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) are 
paying rich dividends as we move towards full compliance 
with the Act and Rules thereunder.
2. Fire Safety and Emergency Preparedness
 During the year, there were number of media reports 
on serious fire incidents in multiple hospitals across the 
country. Given the inherent difficulties and risks involved 
in evacuating critical patients, prevention is the only 
practical option in mitigating the fire risk.  At NH, in the 
last 2-3 years, we have gone the extra mile to invest in 
infrastructure upgrades, fire-resistant materials, and 
regular training including mock drills etc. to foster a culture 
of vigilance and prevention across all facilities.3. Environmental and Climate Risks
 We recognize the growing impact of climate change 
and environmental regulations. NH is enhancing energy 
efficiency, water conservation, and biomedical waste 
management practices to reduce environmental footprint 
and ensure regulatory compliance.
4. Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery
 As an essential 24X7 service provider, NH continues to 
invest in developing robust business continuity plans to 
ensure uninterrupted operations during pandemics, natural 
disasters, or IT outages. These include scenario planning, 
backup systems, and crisis communication protocols.
5. Supply Chain and Vendor Management
 The ongoing Ukraine and now the Iran war situation 
continues to disrupt supply chain across the world.  We 
surely are not immune from those impacts. Our focus is 
to improve resilience by vendor diversification, increased 
and closer monitoring of life saving and critical supplies as 
well as implementing risk-based vendor assessments to 
predict and reduce disruptions.
6. Reputational Risk
 While NH continues to invest in achieving and 
maintaining the highest Quality Accreditations to ensure 
enhanced clinical outcomes and patient experiences, we 
acknowledge that public and media perception are equally 
central to our reputation. Continuous monitoring tools are 
deployed to receive and quickly respond to inputs from 
feedback channels, social media, and media coverage to 
proactively manage reputational risks.
7. Workforce and Talent Management
 In healthcare, the greatest asset are our people. NH 
invests in continuous training, employee well-being, and 
leadership development to mitigate workforce-related 
risks. The consultant doctors, nurses and other medical 
support technicians’ community at NH are recognized and 
respected as the most important stakeholders in ensuring 
excellence in delivery of health care.

8. Technology Obsolescence

9. Expansion and Integration Risks

19. BUSINESS RESPONSIBILITY AND 
SUSTAINABILITY REPORT (BRSR)
 In November 2018, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) 
constituted a Committee on Business Responsibility 
Reporting (“the Committee”) to finalize business 
responsibility reporting formats for listed and unlisted 
companies, based on the framework of the National 
Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC). 
Through its report, the Committee recommended that BRR 
be rechristened BRSR, where disclosures are based on 
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) parameters, 
compelling organizations to holistically engage with 
stakeholders and go beyond regulatory compliances in 
terms of business measures and their reporting. SEBI, vide 
its circular dated May 10, 2021, made BRSR mandatory for 
the top 1,000 listed companies (by market capitalization) 
from the financial year 2024.
 The Board of Directors of the Company has adopted

33. NAMES OF COMPANIES WHICH HAVE 
BECOME OR CEASED TO BE COMPANY’S 
SUBSIDIARIES, JOINT VENTURES OR 
ASSOCIATE COMPANIES DURING THE YEAR 
 Companies which have become subsidiaries
 i. Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd.
  Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd. is a wholly-owned 
subsidiary of Health City Cayman Islands Limited, 
Cayman Islands and a step-down subsidiary of the 
Company incorporated in the United Kingdom on 
October 8, 2025. The Company was incorporated 
to act as a holding Company for potential future 
investments that the subsidiary may explore in 
geographies outside of Cayman Islands. Narayana 
Hrudayalaya UK Ltd. holds 100% of the equity 
investments in Practice Plus Group Hospitals Limited, 
the operating subsidiary in the United Kingdom. 
 ii. Practice Plus Group Hospitals Ltd.
  Health City Cayman Islands Limited, a wholly-owned 
subsidiary in Cayman Islands, through its wholly-
owned subsidiary, Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd. 
in the United Kingdom has acquired 100% equity 
shares of Practice Plus Group Hospitals Ltd., (a 
Company incorporated in the United Kingdom) on 
November 6, 2025. The acquisition of Practice Plus 
Group Hospitals Ltd. will build upon the international 
presence of Narayana Health, following the successful 
expansion in the Caribbean through Health City 
Cayman Islands. Practice Plus Group Hospitals Ltd. 
runs and operates 7 hospitals, 3 Surgical Centers, 
2 Urgent Treatment Centers, 3 Musculoskeletal/
Diagnostic Centers and 1 Ophthalmology Center with 
330 bed capacity in the United Kingdom. 
 iii. Practice Plus Group Property Ltd.
  Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd., a wholly-owned 
step-down overseas subsidiary of the Company 
has incorporated a new wholly-owned subsidiary Company, namely, Practice Plus Group Property 
Ltd. on March 11, 2026 under the laws of the United 
Kingdom. The subsidiary is incorporated with object 
to acquire, hold, develop and maintain immoveable 
(land & building) hospital infrastructure in the United 
Kingdom. Such facilities shall be exclusively used 
captively by hospital operating entities of NH Group in 
UK, generally referred to as Opco / Propco structure. 
Currently, Practice Plus Group Hospitals Limited runs 
and operates hospitals in the United Kingdom. 
 iv. Narayana Healthcare North Private Limited
  The Company has incorporated a wholly-owned 
subsidiary, Narayana Healthcare North Private Limited 
on January 16, 2026. The wholly-owned subsidiary is 
incorporated to carry on the business of healthcare 
services in the field of operation of hospitals, health 
and wellness management. With the Company having 
gained foothold in the Northern part of the country 
and after considering the latent potential to optimise 
the presence in the region, the new wholly-owned 
subsidiary was incorporated to have a focused and 
dedicated entity for the business in the region.
 v. Shepton Mallet Health Partnership Limited
  Shepton Mallet Health Partnership Limited (SMHPL) 
was set up as an intermediary relating to the Shepton 
Mallet Joint Venture. Practice Plus Group Hospitals 
Limited (a wholly-owned subsidiary of Narayana 
Hrudayalaya UK Ltd., United Kingdom) owns 51% stake 
in Shepton Mallet Health Partnership Limited, with the 
remaining shares being held by Somerset Partnership 
NHS Foundation Trust. SMHPL is a subsidiary of 
Practice Plus Group Hospitals Limited and a step-down 
subsidiary of the Company.
34. AMALGAMATION OF MERIDIAN MEDICAL 
RESEARCH & HOSPITAL LTD., A SUBSIDIARY 
WITH NARAYANA HRUDAYALAYA LIMITED 
(HOLDING COMPANY) 
 During the financial year under review, the stock 
exchanges, BSE Limited and National Stock Exchange 
of India Limited, after reviewing the scheme has issued 
their ‘No Observation’ letter in June 2025 for the proposed 
merger of Meridian Medical Research & Hospital Ltd. 
(MMRHL), a subsidiary with the Company. Post receipt 
of No Observation letter from the stock exchanges, an 
application has been filed by the Company and MMRHL 
with the Hon’ble National Company Law Tribunal, 
Bengaluru Bench (Hon’ble NCLT) seeking its approval for 
the amalgamation of MMRHL with the Company. 
 Pursuant to the Order dated December 2, 2025 passed by 
the Hon’ble NCLT, Bengaluru Bench, the meetings of the 
Shareholders and Creditors (Secured and Unsecured) were 
convened on January 19, 2026 for seeking their approval

Regulatory authorities for seeking their ‘No Objection’

NH Integrated Care Private Limited (NHIC), a wholly-
owned subsidiary, an application has been filed by the 
Company and NHIC with the Hon’ble National Company 
Law Tribunal, Bengaluru Bench (Hon’ble NCLT) seeking its 
approval of the draft Scheme of Arrangement between NH 
Integrated Care Private Limited (‘Demerged Company’), 
Narayana Hrudayalaya Limited (‘Resulting Company’) 
and their respective shareholders and creditors, i.e. to 
demerge the clinic operations of NHIC and merging the 
same with the Company. 
 Pursuant to the Order dated February 13, 2026 passed by 
the Hon’ble NCLT, Bengaluru Bench, the meetings of the 
Shareholders and Creditors (Secured and Unsecured) were 
convened on April 2, 2026 for seeking their approval of 
the draft scheme of arrangement between the Demerged 
Company, Resulting Company and their respective 
shareholders and creditors. The special resolutions were 
passed by the shareholders and the creditors with more 
than requisite majority and the final petition was filed 
by the Company with the Hon’ble NCLT in April 2026. 
Notices were dispatched to all the Regulatory authorities 
for seeking their ‘No Objection’ with respect to above-
mentioned scheme of arrangement. Upon receipt of No-
Objection letters from the Regulatory Authorities and 
basis the hearings, the Final Order by the Hon’ble NCLT is 
expected to be received in due course.

1. Brief outline of Narayana Hrudayalaya CSR 
Policy (NH CSR):
 Narayana Hrudayalaya Limited aims to make a positive 
difference in the lives of the people by engaging in activities 
that eliminates or alleviates pain and suffering to the under 
privileged sections of the society by:
	 Promoting healthcare facilities for the upliftment of 
people at large and creating a positive impact by 
addressing issues of accessibility and affordability.
	 Promoting educational facilities to help and assist in 
unfolding the creative potentials and talents of the 
children and amateurs.
	 Strive for socio-economic development thereby 
reducing inequality between rich and poor.
1.1. Overview of projects/programs undertaken during 
the financial year 2025-26
 EDUCATION PROGRAM - UDAAN
The Udaan scholarship program was started in December 
2014 in Karnataka with an objective to nurture the potential 
of rural students from disadvantaged backgrounds and 
create a platform which they could leverage towards 
realizing medical education and become Doctors. 
Students from our Udaan program can be motivated to 
use their medical education in improving health care 
systems in their villages and small towns. It is hoped 
that these enabled students would fulfil their dreams of 
becoming able physicians, have a multiplier effect among 
students and practice ethical healthcare thereby serving 
the larger community.
The program follows a very careful selection process 
to ensure we are reaching out to the brightest and 
most deserving students who have an aptitude and are 
committed towards taking up science as a subject after 
class X and choosing the medical profession as their 
careers. The social and economic background of the 
students is verified before they become part of our program.
This year 508 Students were supported under the Udaan 
Program for NEET Coaching, 876 MBBS students were 
selected for scholarship program from 15 Government 
Medical colleges and 754 Nursing students were selected 
from 16 Nursing Colleges. The program focuses on 
providing financial support to these young students for NEET 
Coaching, mentoring, and preparing them for the Exam.
India faces a significant need for well-qualified doctors, 
particularly in rural areas. According to the WHO, we 
require a doctor-to-population ratio of 1:1000, which is challenging given the rapidly growing population and 
increasing disease burden in the country. The program 
focuses on providing financial support for NEET coaching, 
mentoring, and exam preparation, aiming to create 
more doctors from underprivileged backgrounds and 
encourage more students to serve society through nursing 
and MBBS courses.
During FY25, of the 475 students supported under the 
program, 204 students (43%) secured admissions in 
Government Medical Colleges, including 36 students (8%) 
who qualified for AIIMS, underscoring the strong academic 
outcomes and effectiveness of the initiative. 
 FEEDING PROGRAM
 The feeding program aims to provide breakfast in 
Government schools and to support orphanages and 
children’s shelter home with basic meal supplements. In 
collaboration with local NGOs and Clubs the program 
supported over 3,746 children during this year across 27 
schools in four states. It was observed that there is an 
increase in school attendance due to improvement in Body 
Mass Index (BMI) and overall weight of students. The main 
objective of the program is provide breakfast for children 
studying in Government schools, as well as extend the 
support to orphanages, old age homes with the help of 
local NGOS and social organizations. This project will 
continue this year, with plans to reach more government 
schools and orphanages for broader coverage.
PROVIDING SAFE DRINKING WATER AND SANITATION 
FACILITIES
 The Project was initiated in Government schools for 
improving basic facilities related to safe drinking water and 
providing toilets in Government schools. It was observed 
that majority of girls students were not attending schools 
due to unavailability of basic toilets and change facilities 
in schools, also drinking water facilities were not present 
in these schools and thus students were falling sick with 
water borne diseases which lead to poor attendance 
and dropouts in Government schools.The project led to 
measurable improvement in school attendance, with a 
notable positive impact on female student participation, 
driven by enhanced sanitation infrastructure. In FY26, the 
program covered 73 Government schools, benefiting over 
51,000 students. Against a total impact base of 10,220 
students, the initiative achieved 20% direct beneficiary 
impact during the year. The program was executed across 
eight states, reflecting strong scale and outreach.Annexure III
