 Ind AS 108 “Operating Segment” (“Ind AS 108”) establishes standards for the way that public business enterprises report 
information about operating segments and related disclosures about products and services, geographic areas, and major 
customers. Based on the “management approach” as defined in Ind AS 108, Operating segments are to be reported in a 
manner consistent with the internal reporting provided to the Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM). The CODM evaluates the 
Group’s performance and allocates resources on overall basis. The Group’s operating segments are ‘Medical and Healthcare 
related Services’ and Others (Insurance Segment).

38 Leasehold land includes 36 acres of land acquired by Narayana Hospitals Private Limited ("NHPL") in the year 2008 under 
perpetual lease from Government of Gujarat amounting to H 1,652.38 million. The aforesaid land has been granted to NHPL 
by Government of Gujarat at a concessional rate under Gujarat Health Project for construction of heart hospital with certain 
conditions including but not limited to the following:
 - 1,000 bed hospital for cardiac surgery should be built and be operational within 18 months from the date of completing legal 
formalities/ handing over with clear title and after obtaining all necessary permissions from all concerned departments. 
Self dependent 100 seat medical college under Medical Council of India (‘MCI’) Rules should be built and be operational 
within 36 months. Total project including 5,000 bed super-specialty hospital should be completed within 6 years;
 - Self dependent medical college, to be established by NHPL, should be set up with total adherence to rules governed by 
MCI and Government of India;
 - 5% surgery in the proposed health city should be done free. Only medicines and disposables should be charged;
 - 20% cardiac surgeries should be performed at the subsidised rate of H 0.07 million only, which includes every expense;
 - Beneficiaries of the above said 5% and 20% surgeries will be referred by the Government of Gujarat;
 - 15% out-patients should be given free consultation. Diagnostics fees will be charged at 50%;
 - After achieving, 5,000 surgeries annually, 1,000 surgeries should be performed under concessional rate of H 0.07 million 
and 250 surgeries should be performed free and
 - Number of student intake and fees for the proposed medical college should be according to the prevailing government rules.
 NHPL was unable to start the project on the specified date and received a show cause notice from the Government of Gujarat 
on 22 December 2010. Subsequent to the show cause notice, NHPL replied on 19 January 2011 assuring the Government of 
Gujarat that the entire project will be completed by June 2016.
 As per the letter dated 19 January 2011, the timelines committed by NHPL are as follows:
Commissioning timelines
a) 500 bed multispecialty hospital June-2012
b) 1000 bed multispecialty hospital (expansion) June-2012
c) 100 seat Medical College June-2013
d) 5000 bed Health City June-2016
 The Company commenced operations in its Ahmedabad unit on 03 May 2012. As of 31 March 2026, the Group is yet to achieve 
the above timelines. The Group based on its past projects with government and other authorities believes that the terms/ 
conditions of grant of leasehold land at concessional rate would be renegotiated and no liability or adjustment to recorded 
assets is required as at 31 March 2026.

to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 202639 In the year 2008-09, NHPL was allotted 35 acres of land by Jaipur Development Authority (‘JDA’) for establishing a medical 
college at Bagrana Grama, Jaipur (""Bagrana""). Subsequently, NHPL has surrendered 25 acres of land to JDA and retained 10 
acres of land. However, in the year 2013-14 JDA intimated NHPL that 6,000 sq. meters of land out of the 10 acres land retained 
will be utilised for the completion of ring road project. Subsequently, JDA gave another proposal of land allotment at Govind 
Pura Ropada, in lieu of 10 acres at Bagrana, NHPL gave its consent on the same through letter dated 14 April 2015.
 Since this land is given in lieu of land allotted at Bagrana, NHPL has requested JDA that the land at Govind Pura Ropada to be 
valued the same as it was during the time of allotment of land in Bagrana in March 2008.
 As at 31 March 2026, NHPL had paid H 54.44 million (31 March 2025: H 54.44 million) to JDA and accrued the balance payable of  
H 77.11 million (31 March 2025: H 71.18 million). NHPL would capitalize this amount along with any other payment once NHPL 
gets the land registered in its name. As at 31 March 2026, NHPL has assessed the status of the advance paid and on grounds 
of prudence has recorded a provision for the above advance amounting to H 54.44 million. The Company continues to engage 
with JDA for resolution of the above.

41 Discontinued Operations
 Narayana Vaishno Devi Specialty Hospitals Private Limited ("NVDSHPL")
 NVDSHPL had entered into a Concessionaire Agreement with Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board ("the trust") to operate, 
maintain and manage a 230 bed multi specialty hospital on public private partnership model. NVDSHPL is required to pay 
concession fees to trust as mutually agreed, during the period of agreement. The trust has invested and incurred capital costs 
to set up/ establish 230 bed multi specialty hospital and has reimbursed costs incurred by NVDSHPL for providing technical 
assistance during the refurbishment and commissioning period to the extent of H 5 million. The period of agreement was 21 
Years from the Commercial Operation Date (COD) which is April 2016.
 Narayana Vaishno Devi Speciality Hospitals Private Limited (NVDSHPL), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Company was 
running and operating the Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Narayana Superspeciality Hospital at Kakryal near Katra in Jammu which 
caters to patients across more than 20 different specialties, with radiology, obstetrics & gynaecology, oncology, etc. upto the 
closing hours of 31 March 2026. Pursuant to the Business Transition Agreement dated 25 March 2026 and the Management 
Agreement dated 28 March 2025, the business undertaking of Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Narayana Superspeciality Hospital has 
been transferred on a going concern basis to Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Charitable Society (SMVDCS). Accordingly, with effect 
from 01 April 2026, the ownership, operations and control of the Hospital stand vested with SMVDCS, and the subsidiary 
continues to provide management and consultancy support in terms of the applicable agreements. Consequent to the 
aforesaid management agreement, the Company has assessed the carrying value of assets and liabilities to be transferred with 
recoverable value and written down an amount of H 62.06 million (H 83.63 million in previous year) which has been considered 
as loss on disposal of discontinued operations for the year ended 31 March 2026.
 Consequent to the above, the operations of NVD are considered as Discontinued operations and the impact of the same is

to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 2026 B. Financial risk management
  The Group's activities expose it to a variety of financial risks: credit risk, market risk and liquidity risk.
  (i) Risk management framework
   The Group's risk management is carried out by a central treasury department under policies approved by the Board 
of Directors. The Board supervises overall risk management, as well as policies covering specific areas, such as 
foreign exchange risk, credit risk and use of financial instruments.
  (ii) Credit risk
   Credit risk is the risk that the counterparty will not meet its obligation under a financial instrument or customer contract, 
leading to financial loss. The credit risk arises principally from its operating activities (primarily trade receivables) and 
from its investing activities, including deposits with banks and financial institutions and other financial instruments.
   Credit risk is controlled by analysing credit limits and creditworthiness of customers on a continuous basis to whom 
credit has been granted after obtaining necessary approvals for credit. The collection from the trade receivables are 
monitored on a continuous basis by the receivables team.
   The Group establishes an allowance for impairment that represents its estimate of expected losses in respect of trade 
and other receivables based on the past and the recent collection trend. The maximum exposure to credit risk as at 
reporting date is primarily from trade receivables amounting to H 7,426.89 million (previous year: H 6,353.45 million). 
The movement in allowance for impairment in respect of trade and other receivables during the year was as follows:
(H in million)

   No single customer accounted for more than 10% of the revenue as of 31 March 2026 and 31 March 2025. There is 
no significant concentration of credit risk.
   Credit risk on cash and cash equivalents is limited as the Group generally transacts with banks and financial 
institutions with high credit ratings assigned by international and domestic credit rating agencies.
  (iii) Liquidity risk
   Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial 
liabilities that are settled by delivering cash or another financial asset. The Group’s approach to managing liquidity is 
to ensure, as far as possible, that it will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they are due, under both 
normal and stressed conditions, without incurring unacceptable losses or risking damage to the Group’s reputation.

to the Consolidated Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 202653 On 21 November 2025, the Government of India notified provisions of the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 
2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (collectively 
referred to as the “Labour Codes”). These Labour Codes consolidate twenty-nine existing labour laws into a unified framework 
governing employee benefits during and post-employment. The Labour Codes amongst other things introduced changes 
including a uniform definition of wages and enhanced benefit to leave.
 The Group has assessed the financial implications of these changes which has resulted in increase in gratuity liabilities and 
leave liabilities arising out of past service cost by H 509.54 million. As the impact arises from the enactment of new legislation 
and is considered non-recurring in nature, the Group has presented this incremental amount under “Exceptional Item” in the 
year ended 31 March 2026. The Group continues to monitor developments related to the Labour Codes and will evaluate any 
further implications on the measurement of employee benefit liabilities and will incorporate appropriate accounting treatment 
based on these developments as required.

CARBON NEUTRAL ROADMAP 
& CLIMATE RESILIENCE
Narayana Health has set a Carbon Neutrality Target for 2040, building a robust GHG emissions baseline across Scope 1, Scope 2, 
and Scope 3, aligned with India’s NDCs under the Paris Agreement and UN SDGs.
At Narayana Health, the journey toward sustainable healthcare is guided by continuous engagement with key stakeholders, including 
investors, regulators, employees, patients, partners, and industry bodies. Their feedback helps shape our sustainability priorities 
and supports transparent communication through disclosures such as the Integrated Annual Report, Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report (BRSR), sustainability reports, investor presentations, and the corporate website. Through collaborations with 
the Health & Environment Leadership Platform (HELP), Consortium of Accredited Healthcare Organizations (CAHO), Association of 
Healthcare Providers (India) (AHPI), Health Care Without Harm (HCWH), and Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP), 
Narayana Health stays connected to evolving best practices and collectively addresses key challenges including climate resilience, 
water stewardship, and waste management.

ENERGY & EMISSIONS 
MANAGEMENT
Narayana Health continuously monitors electrical energy consumption with digital energy monitoring systems, heat sensor-based 
controls, and targeted investments in energy-efficient equipment upgrades. Employee awareness programs on energy efficiency 
run on the in-house Ed-Spark platform.
Having exceeded the earlier 35% renewable electricity target, Narayana Health has revised its ambition upward. Karnataka hospitals 
lead the way, powered primarily by a 15.48 MWp Solar Park generating 22–23 Million Units (MUs) annually, supplemented by 4–5 
MUs from hydro and wind contracts — totalling 26–28 MUs of renewable power per year.
	 Transitioning diesel-fired boilers to modern refrigerant-based heat pumps — significantly reducing direct emissions
	 Battery-powered cars and carts for internal patient, staff, and visitor transport — eliminating stationary vehicle emissions
	 Upgrading old pumps and cooling towers with advanced energy-efficient technologies
	 Progressive upgrade of air conditioners and chillers to environmentally friendly refrigerants — reducing ODS fugitive emissions
	 Regular energy efficiency evaluations and lifecycle cost analyses for all technology upgrades
	 Installing Retrofit Emission Control Devices (RECDs) for existing DG sets; all new DG sets comply with CPCB emission normsTotal Energy Consumption UoM FY 2022~23 FY 2023~24 FY 2024~25 FY 2025~26

CIRCULAR ECONOMYGOING PAPERLESSWater stewardship is integral to sustainable healthcare. Narayana Health focuses on efficient water use through continuous monitoring, 
water audits, conservation measures, rainwater harvesting, and wastewater treatment and reuse.
Narayana Health’s waste management approach follows a structured process — segregation at source, responsible collection, secure 
in-house transport (including barcoding for biomedical waste), and disposal only through authorized vendors. Regular Annual Waste 
Management Audits assess compliance and identify improvement areas.Digital healthcare is reducing paper consumption across operations through EMRs, the Narayana Health Care App, digital discharge 
summaries, and digitization of insurance, pharmacy, and administrative processes.

Guided by a Zero Harm vision, Narayana Health has implemented comprehensive OHS SOPs across all facilities covering electrical 
safety, fire safety, needle-stick injury prevention, workplace violence, and laser safety. The OHS Management System is aligned with 
NABH and JCI standards, supported by regular HVA exercises, AERB and NACO guideline adherence, dedicated safety committees, 
role-based health screenings, and vaccination drives.
	 HMIS–ATHMA integrated incident reporting with Root Cause Analysis (RCA) for every case
	 More than 473 clinical and 983 non-clinical mock drills are conducted annually to regularly assess staff readiness, validate 
emergency protocols, and test the operational status of essential equipment.In FY 2025–26, Udaan (NEET, Nursing, MBBS) expanded to 21 colleges across Karnataka, Maharashtra, Jammu, Gujarat, Rajasthan, 
and West Bengal, supporting 508 underprivileged NEET students — 46% of whom were girls. Implemented in 41 designated 
Aspirational Districts across 14 states.

Zero Harm — Embedded across all 
Narayana Health facilities and operations
Launched in December 2014, the Udaan scholarship programme empowers meritorious students from rural and economically

has enabled students from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, including scholars such as Akshit Gangwar from Bareilly and 
Kunal from Faridabad, to pursue their aspirations of becoming doctors and serving underserved communities despite significant 
financial and personal challenges.

NARAYANA HEALTH ACADEMIC 
PROGRAM
CASE STUDY: Narayana Health operates one of India’s largest healthcare academic ecosystems, with over 140 Diplomate of National Board (DNB) 
programmes across 35 affiliations. Through the Narayana Hrudayalaya Foundation (NHF) and Asia Heart Foundation (AHF), academic 
programmes are offered across Medicine, Nursing, Physiotherapy, and Allied Health Sciences. Combining classroom learning with 
hands-on clinical exposure in multi-specialty hospital environments, these institutions help strengthen the healthcare talent pipeline 
and develop skilled, compassionate healthcare professionals.14,930+
Doctors, Nurses & Paramedical Staff 
Trained
At Narayana Health, we believe that access to advanced healthcare should not be limited by geography, financial circumstances, or 
the complexity of a medical condition. Through pioneering clinical expertise, innovative treatment approaches, and patient-centric 
support systems, we continue to deliver life-changing outcomes for patients facing some of the most challenging health conditions. 
The following stories highlight how our commitment to clinical excellence and compassionate care is transforming lives across India.
Narayana Health achieved a significant milestone in paediatric heart failure care by successfully supporting three critically ill teenagers 
with Ventricular Assist Devices (VADs) while they awaited heart transplants. Each patient was admitted with end-stage heart failure, 
facing a critical risk to survival and requiring immediate intervention.
To stabilise their condition, multidisciplinary teams implanted advanced mechanical heart pumps that temporarily took over the 
function of their failing hearts, providing vital support while suitable donor hearts were identified. Despite the challenges associated 
with organ availability, compatible donor hearts were found within 28 to 45 days, enabling all three patients to undergo successful 
heart transplants.
The cases included a teenager requiring support for both sides of the heart, a patient diagnosed with severe dilated cardiomyopathy, 
and a childhood cancer survivor who later developed heart failure. All three patients have since recovered and returned home. This 
achievement demonstrates Narayana Health’s capability in delivering highly specialised paediatric cardiac care while advancing 
access to complex, life-saving therapies in India.Transforming Lives Through Advanced, Accessible Care
A New Lease on Life Through Advanced Heart Failure Care
Narayana Health’s Bone Marrow Transplant (BMT) programme continues to transform the lives of children living with thalassemia by 
providing access to curative treatment and long-term hope. Through awareness initiatives, free HLA testing camps, donor-matching 
programmes, and financial assistance supported by government and CSR initiatives, children from underserved communities across 
the country are able to access advanced transplant care.Expanding Access to Curative Treatment for Children with ThalassemiaTo date
